'''Basketball at the Summer Olympics''' has been a [[sport]] for men consistently since [[Basketball at the 1936 Summer Olympics|1936]]. Prior to its inclusion as a medal sport, [[basketball]] was held as an unofficial demonstration event in [[Basketball at the 1904 Summer Olympics|1904]] and [[Basketball at the 1924 Summer Olympics|1924]]. Women's basketball made its debut in the [[Summer Olympics]] in [[Basketball at the 1976 Summer Olympics|1976]]. [[FIBA]] organizes both the men's and women's [[FIBA World Olympic Qualifying Tournament]]s and the Summer Olympics basketball tournaments, which are sanctioned by the [[International Olympic Committee|IOC]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.fiba.basketball/presentation |title=Presentation |publisher=FIBA.basketball}}</ref>

The United States is by far the most successful country in Olympic basketball, with [[United States men's national basketball team|United States men's teams]] having won 17 of 20 tournaments in which they participated, including seven consecutive titles from [[Basketball at the 1936 Summer Olympics|1936]] through [[Basketball at the 1968 Summer Olympics|1968]]. [[United States women's national basketball team|United States women's]] teams have won 10 titles out of the 12 tournaments in which they competed, including eight in a row from [[Basketball at the 1996 Summer Olympics|1996]] to [[Basketball at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament|2024]]. Besides the United States, [[Argentina national basketball team|Argentina]] is the only nation still in existence which has won either the men's or women's tournament. The [[Soviet Union national basketball team|Soviet Union]], [[Yugoslavia national basketball team|Yugoslavia]] and the [[Unified Team at the 1992 Summer Olympics|Unified Team]] are the countries no longer in existence who have won the tournament. The United States are the defending champions in both men's and women's tournaments.

On 9 June 2017, the Executive Board of the International Olympic Committee announced that [[3x3 basketball]] would become an official Olympic sport as of the [[2020 Summer Olympics]] in [[Tokyo]], Japan, for both men and women.<ref>{{Cite web|date=29 April 2021|title=Tokyo 2020 event programme to see major boost for female participation, youth and urban appeal |url=https://olympics.com/ioc/news/tokyo-2020-event-programme-to-see-major-boost-for-female-participation-youth-and-urban-appeal |access-date=21 June 2021 |publisher=International Olympic Committee|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=IOC adds 3-on-3 basketball to 2020 Olympics |url=http://www.nba.com/article/2017/06/09/ioc-votes-include-3-3-basketball-2020-tokyo-olympics#/ |access-date=10 November 2017 |publisher=National Basketball Association |date=9 June 2017}}</ref>

==History==
[[Basketball]] was invented by [[James Naismith]] in [[Springfield, Massachusetts]], in 1891. Within a few decades, the new game became popular throughout the United States as an indoor sport. The popularity spread overseas and the [[International Basketball Federation]] (FIBA) was organized in 1932 in [[Geneva]], Switzerland. The [[YMCA|Young Men's Christian Association]] (YMCA) had a big part in the spread of this sport to many countries, and as many as 21 teams competed in the first Olympic basketball tournament.<ref name=dream>{{cite news
|url=https://olympics.com/en/news/olympic-basketball-history-dream-team-usa-soviet-union|title=History of basketball at Olympics: A tale of American domination|work=Olympics|author=Naveen Peter|date=11 February 2023|access-date=6 March 2023}}</ref>

===American dominance===
Thanks in part to the effort of [[Phog Allen]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.slamonline.com/online/blogs/2008/08/before-they-were-giants/ |title=Before They Were Giants |website=SLAM |date=20 August 2008}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.hoophall.com/halloffamers/bhof-phog-allen.html|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20071230130907/http://www.hoophall.com/halloffamers/bhof-phog-allen.html|url-status=dead|title=Basketball Hall of Fame&nbsp;– Phog Allen|archivedate=30 December 2007}}</ref>—a [[Kansas Jayhawks men's basketball|Kansas Jayhawks]] collegiate coach—the first Olympic basketball tournament was organized in the [[Basketball at the 1936 Summer Olympics|1936 Berlin Olympics]] on outdoor tennis courts. Dr. Naismith presented the medals to the top three teams. According to the Olympic rules of that time, all of the competitors were amateurs. The tournament was held indoors for the first time in [[Basketball at the 1948 Summer Olympics|1948]]. The [[United States men's national basketball team|American team]] proved its dominance, winning the first seven Olympic tournaments through [[Basketball at the 1968 Summer Olympics|1968]], without losing a single game. While the Americans were barred from sending a team that contained players from the professional [[National Basketball Association]], they instead sent in college players; teams from some other countries sent in their best players, as some of their players were classified as "amateur" by FIBA, by earning allowances instead of wages.

===Munich and after===
The U.S. winning streak ended in [[Basketball at the 1972 Summer Olympics|1972]], when the [[Soviet Union national basketball team|Soviet Union]] controversially won the [[1972 Olympic Men's Basketball Final|gold medal game]] against the United States by one point.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://ca.sports.yahoo.com/news/olympics-2021-basketball-scandals-controversy-united-states-soviet-union-031154492.html|title=Biggest Olympic scandals: The most controversial basketball game of all-time}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.history.com/news/epic-sports-upsets-olympics-united-states-soviet-union|title=10 Things You May Not Know About U.S. Basketball's Shocking 1972 Olympics Loss}}</ref>

The U.S. team reclaimed the gold medal in [[Basketball at the 1976 Summer Olympics|1976]], with [[Yugoslavia national basketball team|Yugoslavia]], which had beaten the Soviet Union in the semifinal, finishing runner-up for the second time. In [[Basketball at the 1980 Summer Olympics|1980]], with the Americans' absence due to the [[1980 Summer Olympics boycott|boycott]], Yugoslavia became the third team to win the title, after beating the Soviets anew in the semifinals and [[Italy national basketball team|Italy]] in the final. The Americans regained the title in [[Basketball at the 1984 Summer Olympics|1984]], by beating [[Spain national basketball team|Spain]] in the final, with the Soviets [[1984 Summer Olympics boycott|boycotting]] this time. The Soviets won the gold medal for the second time in [[Basketball at the 1988 Summer Olympics|1988]], after beating the U.S. team for the second time in the semifinal, and the Yugoslavs in the gold medal game.

===Professional era: renewed American dominance===
The advent of the state-sponsored "full-time amateur athlete" of the [[Eastern Bloc]] countries eroded the ideology of the pure [[amateur sports#Olympics|amateur]], as it put the self-financed amateurs of the Western countries at a disadvantage. The [[Soviet Union at the Olympics|Soviet Union]] entered teams of athletes who were all nominally listed in the military, but all of whom were in fact paid by the state to train full-time.<ref name=dream/><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.csmonitor.com/1980/0415/041531.html|title = How the Russians break the Olympic rules|journal = The Christian Science Monitor|date = 15 April 1980}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1974/07/21/archives/soviet-amateur-athlete-a-real-pro-dr-john-nelson-washburn-is-an.html|title=Soviet Amateur Athlete: A Real Pro|newspaper=The New York Times|date=21 July 1974|last1=Washburn|first1=J. N.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.usab.com/history/why-can-pros-complete-in-international-events.aspx|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150120113156/http://www.usab.com/history/why-can-pros-complete-in-international-events.aspx|url-status=dead|archive-date=20 January 2015|title=Why Can Pros Complete in International Events|website=usab.com}}</ref> In April 1989, through the leadership of Secretary General [[Borislav Stanković]], [[FIBA]] approved the rule that allowed [[National Basketball Association|NBA]] players to compete in international tournaments, including the Olympics.<ref name=dream/> In the [[1992 Summer Olympics]], the [[1992 United States men's Olympic basketball team|U.S. "Dream Team"]] [[Basketball at the 1992 Summer Olympics|won the gold medal]] with an average winning margin of 44 points per game, and without calling a timeout. By this time, the [[Soviet Union national basketball team|Soviet Union]] and [[Yugoslavia national basketball team|Yugoslavia]] no longer existed, but their successor states continued to be among the leading forces. Two newly independent countries of the former Yugoslavia and Soviet Union, [[Croatia national basketball team|Croatia]] and [[Lithuania men's national basketball team|Lithuania]], won the silver and bronze medals respectively.

The American team repeated its victory in [[Basketball at the 1996 Summer Olympics – Men's tournament|1996]] and [[Basketball at the 2000 Summer Olympics – Men's tournament|2000]], but its performance was not as dominant as in 1992. Since active NBA players have been allowed to compete in the Summer Olympics, the 1996 Games in [[Atlanta]] is the only instance where the Olympic host city also had a home NBA team — the [[Atlanta Hawks|Hawks]]. [[Serbia national basketball team|Yugoslavia]] was the runner-up in Atlanta, and [[France national basketball team|France]] in [[Sydney]], with Lithuania winning bronze again on both occasions.

The renewed dominance of the U.S. was interrupted in [[Basketball at the 2004 Summer Olympics – Men's tournament|2004]], when the Americans barely made it to the semifinal, after losing to [[Puerto Rico national basketball team|Puerto Rico]] and [[Lithuania men's national basketball team|Lithuania]] in the preliminaries; [[Argentina national basketball team|Argentina]] defeated them in the semifinals, on their way to a gold medal finish, where they beat [[Italy national basketball team|Italy]] in the final, and became the fourth team to win the Olympic title.

The Americans [[2008 United States men's Olympic basketball team|regrouped]] in [[Basketball at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Men's tournament|2008]], beating the reigning [[2006 FIBA World Championship|FIBA world champions]], [[Spain men's national basketball team|Spain]], the gold medal game, with the Argentines beating the Lithuanians in the bronze medal game. The Americans and the Spaniards met again in the [[Basketball at the 2012 Summer Olympics – Men's tournament|2012]] gold medal game, with the [[2012 United States men's Olympic basketball team|U.S.]] again winning, although with the closest winning margin for the American team. The [[2016 United States men's Olympic basketball team|U.S.]] won again in [[Basketball at the 2016 Summer Olympics – Men's tournament|2016]], defeating Serbia in the gold medal game, a rematch of the [[2014 FIBA Basketball World Cup Final]], after eliminating Spain, who settled for bronze. The [[2020 United States men's Olympic basketball team|American team]] defended their title by winning again at the [[Basketball at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Men's tournament|2020 Games in Tokyo]], extending their run to four consecutive gold medal finishes, and seven out of the last eight.

===Women===
The [[Basketball at the 1976 Summer Olympics|first women's tournament]] was staged in the [[1976 Summer Olympics]]. The [[Soviet Union women's national basketball team|Soviet Union]] won five straight games, becoming the inaugural champion. The next two tournaments followed the six-team round-robin format, with the Soviets defending their title in [[Basketball at the 1980 Summer Olympics|1980]] amid the U.S.-led boycott, and the [[United States women's national basketball team|U.S.]] winning in [[Basketball at the 1984 Summer Olympics|1984]], against the [[South Korea women's national basketball team|South Koreans]], amid the Soviet-led boycott. In [[Basketball at the 1988 Summer Olympics|1988]], the tournament expanded into eight teams, with the Americans beating [[Yugoslavia women's national basketball team|Yugoslavia]] in the gold medal game. In [[Basketball at the 1992 Summer Olympics|1992]], the [[Unified Team at the 1992 Summer Olympics#Basketball|Unified Team]], consisting of the former [[Republics of the Soviet Union|Soviet republics]], defeated [[China women's national basketball team|China]] in the gold medal game. In [[Basketball at the 1996 Summer Olympics|1996]], the tournament settled into its current 12-team format; the U.S. has swept all of the tournaments since then, winning 61 consecutive games. Their run represents the longest gold medal streak in Olympic basketball history and the longest period of dominance by any team in an Olympic team sport. During this period, the program featured multiple generations of prominent players, including [[Lisa Leslie]], [[Diana Taurasi]], [[Sue Bird]], [[Tamika Catchings]], and [[Breanna Stewart]]. National teams from countries such as [[Australia women's national basketball team|Australia]], [[Spain women's national basketball team|Spain]], [[France women's national basketball team|France]] and [[China women's national basketball team|China]] emerged as consistent medal contenders during this era amidst the rise of women's basketball worldwide.

==Qualifying==
As of [[Basketball at the 2012 Summer Olympics|2012]], the qualifying process consists of three stages:
#1 team (for each gender) qualifies as the reigning world champion.
#7 teams for men and 5 for women qualify through their respective regional championships.
#3 teams for men and 5 for women qualify through a world qualifying tournament, in which the best teams which did not qualify directly from each zone compete for the remaining berths.

Additionally, the teams of the host nation qualify automatically.

In 2020, the men's tournament will have a new qualification system. After the [[2019 FIBA Basketball World Cup|2019 FIBA World Cup]], seven teams will qualify directly: the top two European and American teams, and the top team from Africa, Asia and Oceania. The next 16 best teams from the FIBA World Cup will join the two teams from each continent at the Olympic qualifiers. It will feature four groups of six teams, where the best team of each group will get the remaining spots at the Olympics. The continental championships will no longer be used for Olympic qualifying.

* The [[Soviet Union national basketball team|Soviet Union]] (as of 1992) and [[Yugoslavia national basketball team|Yugoslavia]] (as of 2006) are defunct. No team carried over the records of these nations.
* [[Yugoslavia national basketball team|Yugoslavia]] has been the designation from two distinct national entities: Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from 1948 to 1988 formed as a joint state of 6 republics; Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from 1996 to 2006 formed as a joint state by only Montenegro and Serbia. In 2003, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was renamed to Serbia and Montenegro, however both Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia and Montenegro represented the same national entity: a joint state of Serbia and Montenegro.

==== Notes ====
:<sup>{{note|1|A}}</sup> The [[National Olympic Committee|NOC]] was not member of the [[International Olympic Committee|IOC]].
:<sup>{{note|1|B}}</sup> As {{flagicon|TWN}} Republic of China/Formosa from 1952 to 1981.
:<sup>{{note|2|B}}</sup> Mainland China as part of {{flagicon|China|1928}} China; Taiwan as part of {{flagicon|Japan|1928}} Japan
:<sup>{{note|3|B}}</sup> As part of {{flagicon|China|1928}} China
:<sup>{{note|3|C}}</sup> Part of {{flagicon|YUG}} Yugoslavia from 1936 to 1988.
:<sup>{{note|4|D}}</sup> Part of {{URS}}.
:<sup>{{note|5|E}}</sup> As {{flagicon|FRG}} West Germany from 1968 to 1988.
:<sup>{{note|6|F}}</sup> Part of {{flagIOC|EUN}} in 1992.
:<sup>{{note|7|G}}</sup> Now {{flagicon|SRB}} Serbia, part of {{YUG}} in 1936–1988, as {{flagIOC|IOP|1992 Summer}} in 1992 and part of {{FR-YUG}} in 1996–2000.
:<sup>{{note|8|H}}</sup> Part of {{SCG}} in 2004.
:<sup>{{note|9|I}}</sup> Part of {{flagicon|MAS}} Malaysia in 1964.
:<sup>{{note|10|J}}</sup> The Soviet Union chose not to compete in 1936 and 1948.
:<sup>{{note|11|K}}</sup> Part of {{flagicon|TCH}} Czechoslovakia from 1920 to 1992.

* [[Yugoslavia national basketball team|Yugoslavia]] has been the designation from two distinct national entities: Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from 1948 to 1988 formed as a joint state of 6 republics; Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from 1996 to 2006 formed as a joint state by only Montenegro and Serbia. In 2003, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was renamed to Serbia and Montenegro, however both Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia and Montenegro represented the same national entity: a joint state of Montenegro and Serbia.
